newsitem.title: INDIA: India should seek free rupee by 2000 - IMF official.
newsitem.headline: India should seek free rupee by 2000 - IMF official.

text.p: India must aim for capital account convertibility of the rupee by 2000, International Monetary Fund (IMF) executive director M.R. Sivaraman said on Thursday.

"By the year 2000 should be our target when most of the regulations we have should go," he told reporters in response to a question on the time by which he thought India should aim for total convertibility of the rupee.
"I personally feel that we are at the right stage to take the steps towards capital account convertibility," Sivaraman said. "We can go step by step."
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram in the 1997/98 (April-March) budget asked the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to set up a panel to chart the path towards capital account convertibility.
"The time is very opportune for India to think in terms of capital account convertibility," Sivaraman said, praising the steps taken by Chidambaram in the budget.
The government must curb inflationary expectations within the economy and leash fiscal deficit, Sivaraman said.
"There has to be a coordinated action between states and centre to contain fiscal deficit," he said.
India aims to reduce its fiscal deficit as a percentage of Gross Domestic Product to 4.5 percent in 1997/98 compared with 5.0 percent in the current fiscal year ending on March 31.
India has to build the institutional framework needed to move towards capital convertibility of the rupee by the year 2000, Sivaraman said.
"We must create an institutional framework for capital account convertibility," he added.
India must modernise its financial market, create a stable money market and improve its banking system in its march towards capital account convertibility, said Sivaraman.
"A fully developed and deep financial market is required."
"In the first phase all restrictions on investment and trade within the country on non-residents should be removed," the senior IMF official said.
This should be followed by a lifting of curbs on Indian investment abroad and on external commercial borrowings.
"In the third phase restrictions on purchases of residential properties by non-residents should be removed," Sivaraman said.
But he warned that the government would have to take various steps to make the rupee stable when the currency is made totally convertibile.
"We have to take various measures to ensure stability," Sivaraman said, when asked about the likely impact of capital convertibility of the rupee.
The rupee was made convertible on the current account of the balance of payments in August 1994. Current account convertibility implies transactions in goods and services.
Capital account convertibility implies the right to transact in financial assets with foreign countries without restrictions.
